title: Odisha's ₹8,300 Crore Coastal Highway to Slash Travel Time to Puri and Konark
excerpt: India's cabinet has approved a 160-km highway along Odisha's coast that will cut travel time by 2.5 hours and accelerate a tourism boom already drawing millions to the state's temples and beaches.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's cabinet approved a ₹8,300 crore coastal highway spanning 160 km in Odisha.
  • The highway will cut travel time by 2.5 hours, enhancing connectivity to Puri and Konark.
  • Odisha welcomed 56 lakh visitors in early 2026, boosting its tourism sector.
  • The project aligns with India's PM GatiShakti plan, connecting nine economic and five logistics nodes.

  • India's cabinet approved a ₹8,300.79 crore coastal highway from Rameshwar to Paradeep spanning 160.18 km across four Odisha districts.
  • The highway will reduce travel time by approximately 2.5 hours, with a design speed of 100 km/h, connecting Puri and Konark to major logistics corridors.
  • Odisha's tourism sector is already surging — 56 lakh visitors arrived in the first five months of 2026, and the Puri-Konark region is being developed as a global destination.
  • The project connects nine economic nodes and five logistics nodes, aligning with India's PM GatiShakti national infrastructure plan.

Cabinet Greenlights Major Coastal Highway

India's Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has approved the construction of a new coastal highway from Rameshwar to Paradeep in Odisha at a capital cost of ₹8,300.79 crore. The 160.18-km road will be built under the Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) and pass through four districts — Khurda, Puri, Kendrapada, and Jagatsinghpur — that form the backbone of Odisha's coastal economy.

The project is divided into two packages. Package 1 covers the 79.40-km Rameshwar-to-Konark stretch as a four-lane, access-controlled highway, with 76.84 km of entirely new greenfield construction. Package 2 runs 80.78 km from Konark to Paradeep as a two-lane highway with paved shoulders — also entirely greenfield, according to The Infra Post.

Designed for a speed of 100 km per hour, the highway is expected to cut travel time between Rameshwar and Paradeep by about 2.5 hours while reducing fuel consumption, carbon emissions, and vehicle operating costs.

Why the Road Matters Now

The existing route to Puri and Konark from Bhubaneswar runs along NH-316, a corridor that officials describe as badly degraded. Nearly 40 percent of the road suffers from ribbon development — shops, homes, and structures built right up to the edge of the carriageway — and is clogged with local commuter traffic, making it unsuitable for long-distance travel, according to the CCEA release.

The existing NH-16, part of the Golden Quadrilateral, already functions as a six-lane highway through Khordha, Bhubaneswar, and Cuttack. But the arteries branching toward the coast have lagged behind, creating a bottleneck at precisely the moment Odisha's tourism sector is booming.

"This landmark project will strengthen connectivity, reduce travel time by nearly 2.5 hours, and create new opportunities for tourism, trade, logistics, and economic growth."

— Mohan Charan Majhi, Chief Minister of Odisha

A Tourism Boom Already Underway

The highway approval lands amid an extraordinary surge in Odisha tourism. More than 56 lakh visitors arrived in the state during the first five months of 2026, drawn by spiritual landmarks like the Jagannath Temple in Puri and the UNESCO-listed Konark Sun Temple, as well as newer attractions along the coast, according to Travel and Tour World.

International visitors from the United Kingdom, United States, Germany, France, Australia, and Japan have contributed to the growth. Officials attribute the momentum to strategic investments in tourism infrastructure, expansion of coastal tourism circuits, development of caravan tourism, and the establishment of water sports and adventure hubs.

The internationally acclaimed Blue Flag beach at Chandrabhaga — near Konark — now offers jet skiing, parasailing, and kayaking. Eco-retreat and glamping facilities at Ramachandi and Balighai are drawing travellers seeking sustainable, nature-based experiences.

Bigger Plans for a Global Destination

The highway is one piece of a broader infrastructure push. In June, Deputy Chief Minister and Tourism Minister Pravati Parida chaired a state-level workshop identifying the Puri-Konark region as a key focus area under the Centre's "One State — One Global Destination" initiative, according to Utkal Daily.

The Puri-Konark corridor is being developed as a heritage, spiritual, and coastal tourism hub centred on Jagannath culture, the Konark Sun Temple, Chilika Lake, and the artisan heritage village of Raghurajpur. During the 2026-27 Odisha Budget, Chief Minister Majhi announced a ₹1,000-crore Shree Jagannath Interpretation Centre in Puri, along with the proposed Shamuka coastal tourism project linked to the upcoming Puri International Airport, according to Outlook Business.

The state has also launched a new branding campaign — "Think India, Think Odisha" — and set a target of attracting 5 crore tourists annually.

What It Means for NRIs and the Diaspora

For members of the Odia diaspora and Indian travellers abroad planning pilgrimages or heritage trips, the highway promises a dramatically improved experience. The current drive from Bhubaneswar to Konark or onward to Puri is notoriously slow and congested — a deterrent for visitors with limited vacation time. A 100 km/h coastal highway, combined with the planned Puri International Airport, could transform the region into a weekend-accessible destination from major Indian metros and a smoother stop on international itineraries.

Hotel occupancy in Puri already hits near-total capacity during the annual Rath Yatra, with premium rooms commanding upwards of ₹50,000 per night. Faster road access is likely to spread visitor traffic more evenly and open up smaller coastal towns to tourism revenue.

What's Next

Construction timelines have not been officially announced, but the project's alignment with PM GatiShakti — India's national infrastructure masterplan — and its Hybrid Annuity funding model suggest a prioritised rollout. The highway will connect nine economic nodes and five logistics nodes, and the government expects a positive impact on the country's Logistics Performance Index.

With Rath Yatra drawing massive crowds every summer and international arrivals climbing, the pressure on Odisha's coastal roads will only increase. Whether the highway arrives fast enough to match the tourism boom it is meant to serve remains the open question.
